[n: Psal. xxv, 8.] And the face of the Lord is the true contemplation and knowledge of divine things according to virtue, seeking which he is taught the cause of his own want and lack. ⟦q16.26|4⟧ For as the face is characteristic of each one, so also spiritual knowledge characterizes the Divine reflectively. ⟦q16.26|5⟧ Which he who seeks is said to seek the face of the Lord. ⟦q16.26|6⟧ But he who is made flesh according to the letter of the law in the bloody sacrifices has a longed-for ignorance, toward only

⟦q17.1|1⟧ [1361] … taking the commandment as pleasure of the flesh, and clinging bodily, according to sense, to the matter alone of the letter.

⟦q17.2|1⟧ 33. ⟦q17.2|2⟧ He who worships bodily according to the Law begets, as matter, sin in activity, and, as form, materially fashions upon it the mind's assent to the pleasures of the senses suited to it. ⟦q17.2|3⟧ But he who receives Scripture spiritually puts to death the activity as matter, and the assent as the form of sin, together with the modes of the misuse of sense for pleasure, through the natural thoughts, on the height of contemplation.

⟦q17.3|1⟧ 34. ⟦q17.3|2⟧ The matter and the form, and the five modes of the five senses that are about the matter and the form by misuse (I mean the passionate and contrary-to-nature entanglement of the senses with sensible things, that is, with the things under time and flux), after the passing-by of the bodily worship in the Law according to the letter, and the crossing-over of ignorance, the spiritual law, or mind, hands over to be put to death by the loftier principles and thoughts of natural contemplation: that these, having come to be on the height of the law of spiritual contemplation, may abolish and put to death the most universal relation, in the symbols, of the things under time toward sense and body.

⟦q17.4|1⟧ 35. ⟦q17.4|2⟧ Without natural contemplation no one discerns the incongruity of the symbols of the Law with respect to divine things. ⟦q17.4|2⟧ For unless one, having first examined naturally the incongruity of divine and intelligible things in the symbols, shall long to come in mind, having put sense wholly outside the divine sanctuaries, to the comeliness of the intelligibles, he cannot be released once for all from the bodily variety in the types; in which, as long as he walks clinging to the letter, he fittingly does not relieve the want that comes from the famine of knowledge, having condemned himself, like the deceiving serpent, to eat the earth of Scripture, that is, its body; [n: Gen. iii, 14.] and not, according to Christ, feeding on the heaven of Scripture, that is, its spirit and soul, which is the heavenly and angelic bread: I mean the spiritual contemplation and knowledge of the Scriptures in Christ, which God gives, abundantly supplied, to those who love him, as it is written: *He gave them the bread of heaven; man did eat the bread of angels.* [n: Psal. lxxvii, 24.]

⟦q17.5|1⟧ 36. ⟦q17.5|2⟧ The reception of Scripture by sense toward the body, as being plainly begetting of passions and of the relational disposition toward temporal and flowing things, that is, of the passionate activity of the senses toward sensible things, we must abolish like the children and descendants of Saul, [1364] through natural contemplation on the mountain, that is, in the anagogy of the divine oracles, if indeed we aspire to be filled with divine grace.

⟦q17.6|1⟧ 37. ⟦q17.6|2⟧ The Law understood according to the letter alone wrongs the truth, and so does the people of the Jews, and anyone who is their imitator in understanding, circumscribing the power of the Law by the letter alone, and not admitting, for the manifestation of the mystical knowledge hidden in the letter, natural contemplation, which is the middle between types and truth: leading away from the former those who are being led, and leading them back up to the latter; but as it were denying it altogether, and putting it outside the mystagogy of divine things. ⟦q17.6|2⟧ Those, therefore, who tend the divine spectacles must kill this bodily and temporary reception of the Law, as being under time and flowing, through natural contemplation, as on a mountain, on the height of knowledge.

⟦q17.7|1⟧ 38. ⟦q17.7|2⟧ He utterly abolishes the bodily meaning of Scripture who by practice, through natural contemplation, kills the pleasure-loving and body-loving relation toward unstable and flowing matter that arose in the soul from the written Law; slaughtering, as the children and descendants of Saul, the earth-bound understanding of the Law, through the mediation of natural contemplation, as on a mountain, on the height of knowledge; and making manifest before the Lord, through confession, that is, the former reception of the Law toward the body. ⟦q17.7|3⟧ For this is what the lovers of learning can understand by *to expose to the sun before the Lord*. ⟦q17.7|4⟧ *And they exposed them to the sun*, it says, *on the mountain before the Lord*: [n: ibid. 9.] bringing into the light, through knowledge, that is, the preconception that went astray according to the letter; which is, to make manifest on the height of contemplation that the letter of the Law is dead, through knowledge in the spirit.

⟦q17.8|1⟧ 39. ⟦q17.8|2+3⟧ *The letter*, it says, *kills; but the spirit gives life.* [n: II Cor. iii, 7.] Therefore what is of a nature to kill must be killed by the life-giving spirit. ⟦q17.8|4⟧ For that the bodily element of the Law and the divine, that is, the letter and the spirit, should coexist with each other in activity at once and in the same respect is utterly impossible; since what can take life away is not of a nature even to agree with what provides life according to nature.

⟦q17.9|1⟧ 40. ⟦q17.9|2⟧ The spirit is what bestows life; the letter is what takes life away. ⟦q17.9|3⟧ Therefore the letter and the spirit cannot both act in the same respect, just as the life-giving cannot coexist with the corrupting either.

⟦q17.10|1⟧ [1365] 41. ⟦q17.10|2⟧ Mystical circumcision is the complete removal of the mind's passionate relation to the introduced coming-to-be. ⟦q17.10|3⟧ For, applying ourselves naturally to things, we know that the removal of the integrity which is from God according to nature is not perfection. ⟦q17.10|4⟧ For nature, mutilated by art and through contrivance putting off what belongs to it from God by the principle of its making, does not make perfection; lest we bring in art as stronger than God for the confirming of justice, and make the contrived deficiency of nature a filling-up of a deficiency in justice according to its making. ⟦q17.10|4⟧ But from the local position of the member that is circumcised we are taught to perform by inclination the circumcision of the passionate disposition in the soul; by which the inclination is regulated to run together rather with nature, correcting the passionate law of the acquired coming-to-be.

⟦q17.11|1⟧ 42. ⟦q17.11|2⟧ The foreskin is natural. ⟦q17.11|3⟧ And everything natural is a work of divine making, and very good, according to the voice that says: *And God saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good.* ⟦q17.11|4⟧ But the Law, commanding the foreskin to be removed through circumcision as unclean, brings in God correcting his own work through art, which is most impious even to conceive. ⟦q17.11|5⟧ Therefore he who applies himself naturally to the symbols of the Law knows that God does not correct nature through art, but commands the passible part of the soul that is obedient to reason to be circumcised, which is typically signified through the bodily member; which knowledge, through courage in practice, is of a nature to put away from the inclination. ⟦q17.11|6⟧ For the circumcising priest signifies knowledge, which has, like iron against passion, the courage of reason in practice. ⟦q17.11|7⟧ For the tradition of the Law is abolished when the spirit prevails over the letter.

⟦q17.12|1⟧ 43. ⟦q17.12|2⟧ The Sabbath is rest from the passions and from the motion of the mind about the nature of beings; or complete inactivity of the passions, and universal cessation of the mind's motion about things made, and complete crossing-over to the Divine; in which he who has arrived through virtue and knowledge, as far as is permitted, must not, as with sticks of wood, [n: Num. xv, 32.] take thought for any matter whatever that kindles the passions, nor indeed gather up the principles of nature at all; lest we dogmatize God, after the manner of the Greeks, as delighting in passions or measured by the limits of nature: him whom perfect silence alone has cried aloud, and complete unknowing by way of pre-eminence presents.

⟦q17.13|1⟧ [1368] 44. ⟦q17.13|2⟧ A crown of goodness is pure faith, flowered, after the manner of precious stones, with the lofty utterances of the doctrines and with spiritual words and concepts, binding round the God-loving mind as a head. ⟦q17.13|3⟧ Or rather, the crown of goodness is the very Word of God, who by the variety of the modes of providence and judgement, that is, by self-control over voluntary passions and endurance of involuntary ones, encircles the mind as a head, and by participation in the grace of deification makes the mind itself more beautiful than itself.

⟦q17.14|1⟧ 45. ⟦q17.14|2⟧ Here he says that self-control is a work of Providence, as purifying the passions of inclination; and endurance, he says, is an achievement of judgement, as arrayed against involuntary temptations, and being a symbol of practical philosophy, bringing across to virtue, as from Egypt, from sin, those held fast by it.

⟦q17.15|1⟧ 46. ⟦q17.15|2⟧ It was not because he wished the days to be honoured by men that God commanded the Sabbath and the new moons and the feasts to be honoured; for so he would have decreed, by commandment of the Law, that they worship the creation rather than the Creator, [n: Rom. i, 25.] supposing the days to be venerable by nature and therefore to be worshipped; but he indicated that he himself is honoured symbolically through the days. ⟦q17.15|3⟧ For he himself is the Sabbath, as the rest of the soul from its toils in the flesh and the cessation of labours for justice; the Pasch, as the liberator of those held fast by the bitter slavery of sin; Pentecost, as the beginning and end of beings, and the principle in which all things by nature subsist. ⟦q17.15|4⟧ Consider how the Law destroys those who understand it bodily, persuading them to worship the creation rather than the Creator, and to consider venerable by nature the things that came to be for their sake, having failed to know him for whose sake they themselves came to be.

⟦q17.16|1⟧ 47. ⟦q17.16|2⟧ The world is a limited place and a circumscribed rest; time is a circumscribed motion; whence also the motion of the life of the things in it is subject to alteration. ⟦q17.16|3⟧ But when nature, having passed through place and time in activity and in notion, that is, through the things without which it is not, namely limited rest and motion, is joined immediately to providence, it finds providence to be a principle, simple and stable by nature, and having no circumscription in any way, and therefore no motion at all.

⟦q17.17|1⟧ 48. ⟦q17.17|2⟧ Existing temporally in the world, [1369] nature has its motion subject to alteration, because of the limited rest of the world and the course of time by way of becoming-other; but when it comes to be in God, because of the natural monad of him in whom it has come to be, it will have an unmoved rest and a stable motion-in-sameness, coming to be eternally about the same and one and only; which the word knows to be immediate about the first cause, the abiding foundation of the things made by it.

⟦q17.18|1⟧ 49. ⟦q17.18|2⟧ The mystery of Pentecost is the immediate union of the things provided for with Providence; that is, the union of nature with the principle according to the conception of Providence, in which there is no reflection whatever of time and coming-to-be. ⟦q17.18|3⟧ Again, the Word is our trumpet, as sounding divine and ineffable knowledge into us; the expiation, as, having become like us, dissolving in himself the charges against us, and deifying by the gift of grace in the Spirit the nature that sinned; the feast of Tabernacles, as the practice of our unchangeableness about the good according to the God-imitating habit, and the bond that holds together our transformation into immortality.

⟦q17.19|1⟧ 50. ⟦q17.19|2⟧ He who delights in bare bloody sacrifices, being passionate, prepares those who sacrifice to be zealous about the passions. ⟦q17.19|3⟧ For what genuinely reveres is wont to delight in the things in which what is worshipped delights. ⟦q17.19|4⟧ Hence the word knows as sacrifices rather the slaughter of the passions and the offering of the natural powers: of which the ram is the type of reason; the bull bears the symbol of anger; and the goat is the indication of desire.

⟦q17.20|1⟧ 51. ⟦q17.20|2⟧ We know spiritual sacrifices to be not only the mortification of the passions slaughtered by *the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God*, [n: Ephes. vi, 17.] and the motion by intent, as of blood, of the whole life in the flesh, but also the offering of the habits of philosophy and of all the powers according to nature, dedicated to God and offered whole as a burnt offering by the fire of grace in the Spirit unto the divine lot.

⟦q17.21|1⟧ [1372] 52. ⟦q17.21|2⟧ The earthly meaning of Scripture, when it rules the soul, casts off the natural principles, obliterating them by the misuse of the powers according to nature. ⟦q17.21|3⟧ For this one, while living, truly consumes and persecutes and destroys, circumscribing the Law by the flesh alone, the principles and thoughts according to nature, I mean, honouring as divine the passions of dishonour; [n: Rom. i, 26.] which the thoughts according to nature, receiving licence from the law of the Spirit, kill and put to death together.

⟦q17.22|1⟧ 53. ⟦q17.22|2⟧ As soon as one pursues rationally the philosophy of the virtues, at once he has also naturally transferred the reception of the Scriptures to the spirit, worshipping God practically in newness of spirit through the lofty objects of contemplation, and not in oldness of letter, [n: Rom. vii, 6.] through the lowlier reception of the Law by sense toward the body, becoming, like the Jews, a nurturer of passions and a servant of sin.

⟦q17.23|1⟧ 54. ⟦q17.23|2⟧ As soon as one ceases receiving Scripture by sense toward the body, at once he also runs up in mind toward the spirit through the mediation of nature, doing spiritually those things which the Jew, performing bodily, has God angered.

⟦q17.24|1⟧ 55. ⟦q17.24|2⟧ Every mind lofty and raised up according to God slaughters in the same act both the activity of the passions and the unseemly motion of the thoughts; and besides, the licentious modes of the activity of the senses by misuse. ⟦q17.24|3⟧ For the passions are destroyed by the lofty thoughts of nature, being led in triumph in the lofty contemplation.

⟦q17.25|1⟧ 56. ⟦q17.25|2⟧ The grace of holy baptism is of a nature to abolish the might of sin, that is, *the way of thinking of the flesh*; and obedience in activity to the divine commandments, to kill it with *the sword of the Spirit*, [n: Ephes. vi, 17.] that is, with the word of divine knowledge in the Spirit, crying mystically to the passion of sin, as the great Samuel to Agag: *Because thy sword has made women childless, thy mother shall be made childless today among women.* [n: I Reg. xv, 33.]

⟦q17.26|1⟧ 57. ⟦q17.26|2⟧ The passion of gluttony has made many virtues childless, as with a sword, with the full-grown thought of pleasure. ⟦q17.26|3⟧ For it kills the seeds of temperance through incontinence; it corrupts the equity of justice through greed; it cuts through the continuity from nature of love for man through self-love. ⟦q17.26|4⟧ And to say it briefly, the passion of gluttony is destructive of all the offspring of virtue.

⟦q17.27|1⟧ 58. ⟦q17.27|2⟧ The passion of gluttony is of a nature to kill all the divine offspring of the virtues; but it itself is killed by the grace of faith and by obedience to the divine commandments, through the word of knowledge.

⟦q18.1|1⟧ [1373] 59. ⟦q18.1|2⟧ Our Lord is truly a light of the nations, [n: Luc. ii, 32.] uncovering for them, through true full knowledge, the eyes of the understanding that had closed in the gloom of ignorance; and again having prepared himself for the faithful peoples as a good exemplar of virtue in divine training, becoming for them the outline and sketch of the person that is according to virtue; looking to whom as the author of our salvation, we achieve the virtues by imitation, as far as is possible for us, through practice.

⟦q18.2|1⟧ 60. ⟦q18.2|2⟧ Everyone who out of envy hates, and noises abroad evilly with slanders, him who is stronger in the contests of the virtues and in the abundance of the word of spiritual knowledge, is Saul choked by an evil spirit, not bearing the fame of the better man's blessedness in virtue and knowledge; and raving the more for this reason, that he cannot lay hands on his benefactor. ⟦q18.2|3⟧ And often he even bitterly sends away his dearest Jonathan himself, I mean the innate thought in the conscience, who reproves the unjust hatred and truth-lovingly recounts the achievements of the one hated.

⟦q18.3|1⟧ 61. ⟦q18.3|2⟧ Let us too beseech the intelligible David to play with the lyre of spiritual contemplation and knowledge upon our mind, seized as in a fit by material things, and to drive away the evil spirit of the material vicissitude toward sense, that we may be able to understand the Law spiritually, and find the mystical word hidden in it, and make it a lasting possession as provision for eternal life.

⟦q18.4|1⟧ 62. ⟦q18.4|2⟧ Everyone who yearns for salvation applies himself entirely either to practice or to contemplation. ⟦q18.4|3⟧ For without virtue and knowledge no one has ever in any way been able to attain salvation; since it belongs to virtue to order the motion of the body, reining it back skilfully, as with a kind of bridle, by right thought from its course toward what is out of place; and to contemplation, to decree that what has been well thought and judged be prudently preferred.

⟦q18.5|1⟧ 63. ⟦q18.5|2⟧ Since what thinks is noetic, and what is thought is intelligible, and what is thought is the food and as it were the constitution of what thinks: fittingly God, the bodiless beings being minds, himself being thought, and becoming intelligible to them as far as they reach, illumines them from within, the mind both thinking and being fed.

⟦q18.6|1⟧ 64. ⟦q18.6|2⟧ The intelligible is one thing, and the noetic another. ⟦q18.6|3⟧ For the intelligible is a kind of food, as has been said, of the noetic, [1376] since what is thought, which is intelligible, is greater than what thinks, which is noetic, and is conceived before it. ⟦q18.6|4⟧ For those things are called noetic which, because they are minds, think the intelligibles that lie above them; for the intelligible is what is thought, which is also the food of the noetic, that is, of what thinks.

⟦q18.7|1⟧ 65. ⟦q18.7|2⟧ It must be known that effects have such images of the causes as are possible. ⟦q18.7|3⟧ For effects are all the things brought forth into creation; causes, those that brought them forth; and there is no likeness of these to one another, I mean of causes and effects.

⟦q18.8|1⟧ 66. ⟦q18.8|2⟧ There is no exact likeness between effects and causes; but the effects have such images of the causes as are possible, while the causes themselves are exempt from the effects and are seated above them according to the principle of their own origin. ⟦q18.8|3⟧ For the things of the effects pre-exist in the causes superabundantly and essentially.

⟦q18.9|1⟧ 67. ⟦q18.9|2⟧ Effects are all the things brought forth into creation, whether in heaven or on earth; causes, those that brought them forth, that is, the three hypostases of the holy Trinity. ⟦q18.9|3⟧ It is plain, then, that there is no likeness of these to one another, I mean of causes and effects.

⟦q18.10|1⟧ 68. ⟦q18.10|2⟧ One must know that our mind has, on the one hand, the power for thinking, through which it sees the intelligibles; on the other, the union that surpasses the nature of the mind, through which it is joined to the things beyond itself. ⟦q18.10|3⟧ According to this, then, divine things are to be thought, not in our fashion, but with ourselves wholly standing outside our whole selves and becoming wholly God's. ⟦q18.10|4⟧ For it is better to be God's and not our own. ⟦q18.10|5⟧ For thus will divine things be given to those who come to be with God.

⟦q18.11|1⟧ 69. ⟦q18.11|2⟧ The mind, wishing to think, goes down below itself, descending into intellections. ⟦q18.11|3⟧ For intellections are lower than what thinks, as being thought and comprehended, and fittingly a scattering and partition of the unity of the mind itself. ⟦q18.11|4⟧ For the mind is simple and partless; but intellections are very many and scattered, and as it were forms of the mind. ⟦q18.11|5⟧ Therefore the noetic, that is, the things that think, are less than the intelligibles, that is, the [1377] things thought. ⟦q18.11|6⟧ He calls «union» of the mind, as he says more clearly in what follows, that through which it stretches up to the things beyond itself, that is, applies itself to the contemplation concerning God: namely, to stand outside all sensible and intelligible things, and further also its own motion; and then thus to receive the ray of divine knowledge.

⟦q18.12|1⟧ 70. ⟦q18.12|2+3⟧ If the noetic moves noetically in proportion to itself, it certainly also thinks; if it thinks, it certainly also yearns for what it has thought; if it yearns, it certainly also suffers ecstasy toward it as toward the yearned-for; if it suffers, it is clearly also urged on; if it is urged on, it certainly intensifies the vehemence of its motion; and if it intensifies its motion vehemently, it does not stop until it comes to be whole in the whole yearned-for, and is encompassed by the whole willingly, receiving wholly by choice the saving circumscription, that it may be wholly qualified by the whole that circumscribes it, so that what is circumscribed no longer wishes at all to be able to be known, that very thing, wholly, from itself, but from what circumscribes it: as air wholly illumined by light, and iron wholly fired through by the whole fire, or whatever else there is of the kind.

⟦q18.13|1⟧ 71. ⟦q18.13|2⟧ Great is the relation of those who think to the things thought, and of those who perceive to the sensible things. ⟦q18.13|3⟧ And man, being of soul and of a sensitive body, through his natural relation and property toward each of the two sections of creation by way of interchange, both is circumscribed and circumscribes: the one by essence, the other by power. ⟦q18.13|4⟧ For he is of a nature to be circumscribed by the intelligibles and sensibles, as being soul and body, and to circumscribe them by power, as thinking and perceiving. ⟦q18.13|4⟧ But God is simply and without bound above all beings, both those that contain and those contained, as being utterly without relation to all.

⟦q18.14|1⟧ 72. ⟦q18.14|2⟧ Every pleasure in forbidden things is of a nature to arise entirely from passion, through the mediation of sense, toward some sensible thing. ⟦q18.14|3⟧ For pleasure is nothing other than a form of sense, shaped in the sensitive faculty by some sensible thing; or a mode of sensitive activity, constituted according to irrational desire. ⟦q18.14|4⟧ For desire added to sense turns into pleasure, bringing a form upon it; and sense moved by desire produces pleasure, taking on the sensible thing. ⟦q18.14|5⟧ The saints, then, knowing that the soul, moved contrary to nature toward matter through the mediation of the flesh, puts on the earthly form, themselves moving rather according to nature toward God through the mediation of the soul, resolved to bring the flesh too fittingly into kinship with God, adorning it, as far as possible, through the ascesis of the virtues, with the divine reflections.

⟦q18.15|1⟧ 73. ⟦q18.15|2⟧ The saints, magnificently, according to the true and [1380] infallible mode of motion according to nature, crossed the present age of the wrestling-pits: uniting sense, through the mediation of reason, to the mind that has the simple principles of beings; and bringing to God the mind, purely released from motion about all beings, and quiescent even from its own natural activity; by which mode, gathered wholly toward God, they were counted worthy to be blended, whole, with the whole God through the Spirit, bearing, as far as is possible for men, the whole image of the heavenly, [n: I Cor. xv, 49.] and drawing so much of the divine reflection, if it is lawful to say this, as they themselves, being drawn, were set in God.

⟦q18.16|1⟧ 74. ⟦q18.16|2⟧ They say that God and man are paradigms of each other; and that God is humanized for man through love for man as much as man, having been enabled, has deified himself to God through love; and that man is snatched up by God in mind to the knowable as much as man has manifested through the virtues God, who is invisible by nature.

⟦q18.17|1⟧ 75. ⟦q18.17|2⟧ Everyone who has *put to death his members that are on earth*, [n: Coloss. iii, 5.] and has quenched the whole way of thinking of his flesh, and has shaken off entirely the relation to it through which the love owed by us to God alone is partitioned, and has denied all the tokens of the flesh and the world for the sake of divine grace, so as to be able also to say with the blessed Paul the apostle, *Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?* [n: Rom. viii, 35, 33 [as printed: 'Rom. viii, 33, 35'].] and what follows: such a one has become *without father, without mother, without genealogy*, [n: Hebr. vii, 3.] like the great Melchizedek, having no way to be held fast by flesh and nature, because of the conjunction that has come about with the Spirit.

⟦q18.18|1⟧ 76. ⟦q18.18|2+3⟧ The end of the present life, I think, it is not right to name death, but release from death, separation from corruption, freedom from slavery, cessation of disturbance, destruction of wars, withdrawal of darkness, relief from labours, quiescence of seething, covering of shame, escape from passions, and, to sum up, the limit of all evils; which the saints, achieving through voluntary mortification, presented themselves as strangers and sojourners in life. [n: I Petr. ii, 11.] For fighting nobly against the world and the body and the uprisings from them, and having choked the deceit that comes from both through the entanglement of the senses with sensible things, they kept for themselves the dignity of the soul unenslaved.

⟦q18.19|1⟧ 77. ⟦q18.19|2⟧ A proof, and no small one, that the knowledge of providence has been naturally sown in us, nature itself [1381] gives: whenever, as if pushing us untaught toward God through prayers in sudden distresses, it prepares us to seek salvation from there. ⟦q18.19|3⟧ For seized suddenly by necessity, without choice, before considering anything, we call upon God; as though providence itself were drawing us to itself even without thoughts, and overcoming the swiftness of the noetic power in us, and showing forth the divine help as stronger than all. ⟦q18.19|4⟧ And nature would not lead us without choice toward what has not the nature to come to be; and everything that follows naturally upon anything whatever, as is plain to all, has a strong and invincible power for the demonstration of the truth.

⟦q18.20|1⟧ 78. ⟦q18.20|2⟧ Since of beings some are good and some bad, and these are either present or to come: the good, when expected, one calls desire, and when present, pleasure; and again the evil, when expected, fear, and when present, grief; so that about good things, whether those that truly are or those that are thought to be, there are, and are contemplated, pleasure and desire; and about bad things, grief and fear. ⟦q18.20|3⟧ For desire, when it attains, produces pleasure; when it fails, grief.

⟦q18.21|1⟧ 79. ⟦q18.21|2⟧ They say that all grief is evil by its own nature. ⟦q18.21|3⟧ For even if the earnest man grieves at others' evils, as merciful, yet he does so not antecedently by intent, but consequently by distress; but the contemplative remains passionless even in these, having joined himself to God and alienated himself from all things here.

⟦q18.22|1⟧ 80. ⟦q18.22|2⟧ All the saints, having genuinely laid hold of the divine and unerring word, crossed this age, planting the footprint of the soul on none of the delights in it. ⟦q18.22|3⟧ For they spread out the mind, very fittingly, toward the highest principles about God attainable by men, I mean those of goodness and of love; moved by which, they were taught, God gave being to the things that are and graciously granted well-being: if indeed it is lawful to speak of motion in God, who alone is unmoved, and not rather of wish, which moves all things and brings them into being and holds them together, but is itself in no way ever moved.

⟦q18.23|1⟧ 81. ⟦q18.23|2⟧ The soul, being a noetic and rational essence, both thinks and reasons: having the mind as its power, intellection as its motion, and the concept as its activity. ⟦q18.23|3⟧ For this is the limit of the intellection both of what thinks and of what is thought, as being what bounds the relation of the extremes to each other. ⟦q18.23|4⟧ For the soul, in thinking, [1384] ceases from thinking that which was thought after its intellection of it. ⟦q18.23|5⟧ For what has once been properly thought no longer calls out the power of the soul toward being thought again; and so at each concept it receives rest from the qualified intellection of what was thought, upon the concept.

⟦q18.24|1⟧ 82. ⟦q18.24|2⟧ As ignorance is divisive of those who have gone astray, so the presence of the intelligible light is gathering and unifying of those who are illumined, and perfecting and turning back: turning them back from the many opinions toward what truly is, and gathering the varied sights, or, to speak more properly, imaginings, into one true and pure and uniform knowledge; and filling them with the one and unifying light.

⟦q18.25|1⟧ 83. ⟦q18.25|2⟧ The beautiful is the same as the good, because all things aspire to the beautiful and good for every cause, and there is not any of beings that does not participate in the beautiful and good. ⟦q18.25|3⟧ For to all, the beautiful and good, as truly admirable, is aspired-to and yearned-for and pleasing and to be preferred and beloved. ⟦q18.25|4+5⟧ Note how the divine yearning, pre-existing in the good, begot the good yearning in us, through which we aspire to the beautiful and good, according to him who said: *I became a lover of her beauty.* [n: Sap. viii, 2.] And: *Yearn for her, and she shall keep thee; set a palisade about her, and she shall exalt thee.* [n: Prov. iv, 6.]

⟦q18.26|1⟧ 84. ⟦q18.26|2⟧ The theologians call the Divine sometimes yearning, sometimes love, sometimes yearned-for and beloved. ⟦q18.26|3⟧ Hence, as being yearning and love, it is moved; as yearned-for and beloved, it moves toward itself all things receptive of yearning and love. ⟦q18.26|4⟧ And to say it again more clearly: it is moved as producing an inward relation of yearning and love in those receptive of them; it moves as by nature attractive of the aspiration of the things moved toward it. ⟦q18.26|5⟧ And again it moves and is moved, as thirsting to be thirsted for, and yearning to be yearned for, and loving to be loved.

⟦q18.27|1⟧ 85. ⟦q18.27|2⟧ The divine yearning is also ecstatic, not allowing the lovers to be their own, but the yearned-for's. ⟦q18.27|3⟧ And this the higher show by coming to be in providence for the lesser; those of the same rank, in their mutual cohesion; and the lower, in their more divine turning toward the first. ⟦q18.27|4⟧ Therefore also the great Paul, having come to be possessed by the divine yearning and having partaken of its ecstatic power, says with inspired mouth: *I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me*; [n: Galat. ii, 20.] as a true lover, and as one who has stood outside himself, as he himself says, to God, [n: II Cor. v, 13.] and living not his own life but the life of the yearned-for, as exceedingly beloved.

⟦q18.28|1⟧ 86. ⟦q18.28|2⟧ This too must be dared to be said for the truth's sake:

⟦q19.1|1⟧ [1385] that even he himself, the cause of all things, through the beautiful and good yearning for all things, through the excess of his yearning goodness, comes to be outside himself by his providences toward all the things that are, and is, as it were, charmed by goodness and love and yearning; and from being beyond all things and set apart from all, he is drawn down to being in all, according to an ecstatic superessential power, without departing from himself. ⟦q19.1|2⟧ For this reason those skilled in divine things also call him zealous, as one whose good yearning toward the things that are is great, and as rousing them to zeal for his yearning aspiration, and as showing himself zealous, for whom the things that aspire are also objects of zeal, and as the things that are provided for being objects of zeal to him.

⟦q19.2|1⟧ 87. ⟦q19.2|2⟧ Of love and of yearning they say that he, namely God, is the producer, and, they say, the begetter. ⟦q19.2|3⟧ For he, having these in himself, brought them forth to what is outside, that is, to the creatures; and according to this it is said, *God is love*; and again, *Sweetness and desire*, [n: Cant. v, 16.] which is yearning; and the beloved and the truly yearned-for is he himself. ⟦q19.2|4⟧ By the loving yearning being poured forth from him, then, he himself, its begetter, is said to be moved; and by his being the true object of yearning and beloved and aspired-to and choice-worthy, he moves the things that look toward it, and those in which there is the power of aspiring, proportionately to them.

⟦q19.3|1⟧ 88. ⟦q19.3|2⟧ Think of God, I pray, as procuring and moving toward the yearning conjunction that is in spirit, that is, as its mediator, and as the one who fits things together toward it, so that he is yearned for and loved by his own works. ⟦q19.3|3⟧ And he says *moving*, as moving each thing, according to its own principle, to turn toward him. ⟦q19.3|4⟧ And the name of procuring, even if among those outside it signifies a thing not pure, yet here he says it of the mediation that brings about union in God.

⟦q19.4|1⟧ 89. ⟦q19.4|2⟧ The yearning motion of the good, pre-existing in the good, being simple and unmoved, and proceeding from the good, turns back again to the same, being without end and without beginning; which shows our ever-moving aspiration toward the Divine and [1388] union. ⟦q19.4|2⟧ For the loving union with God is set apart from and lies above every union.

⟦q19.5|1⟧ 90. ⟦q19.5|2⟧ Yearning, whether we should call it divine or angelic or noetic or psychic or natural, let us conceive as a uniting and blending power: moving the higher things to providence for the lower; the coordinate things, again, to a mutual cohesion in communion; and, last of all, the subordinate things to turning toward the better and the superior.

⟦q19.6|1⟧ 91. ⟦q19.6|2⟧ If knowledge unites the knowers and the known, while ignorance is always the cause of change and of division from itself in the one who is ignorant, nothing will move the one who has believed in truth, according to the sacred Word, from the hearth of the true faith; upon which he will have the permanence of unmoved and unchangeable identity. ⟦q19.6|3+4⟧ For he who has been united to the truth knows well that it is well with him, even if the many admonish him as one who is beside himself. [n: II Cor. v, 13.] For it escapes them, as is likely, that he has gone out of error to the truth of the faith that truly is; but he himself truly knows himself to be, not, as they say, raving, but freed, through the simple truth that holds always according to the same things and in the same way, from the unstable and alterable drift about the manifold variety of error.

⟦q19.7|1⟧ 92. ⟦q19.7|2⟧ The saints became good and loving to man, compassionate and merciful, shown to have one disposition of love toward the whole race; by which, having held firm through their whole life the most excellent form of all goods, humility I mean, that which guards the goods and destroys their contraries, they became in no way at all capturable by any of the troublesome temptations, both the voluntary, which fall under the principle of what is in our power, and the involuntary, which are not in our power: by withering, in the case of the former, their uprisings through self-control, and by shaking off, in the case of the latter, their assaults through patience.

⟦q19.8|1⟧ 93. ⟦q19.8|2⟧ The perfect practice of virtue is produced by right faith and unadulterated fear toward God; natural contemplation infallible in its ascent, by firm hope and unblemished intelligence; deification by taking-up, by perfect love and a mind wholly and willingly blinded to the things that are, by transcendence.

⟦q19.9|1⟧ 94. ⟦q19.9|2⟧ The work of practical philosophy, they say, is to render the mind pure of every passionate imagination; that of natural contemplation, to show it expert in all true knowledge of the things that are, according to the cause by which they subsist; and that of theological mystagogy, to make it, by grace, like God and equal, so far as is attainable, according to habit, so that it is no longer at all mindful of anything [1389] of the things after God, because of the transcendence.

⟦q19.10|1⟧ 95. ⟦q19.10|2⟧ What the ether is in the world perceived by sense, that is, the fiery element, this in the world of the understanding is prudence, as a habit illuminating, and receptive of the spiritual principles proper to each of the things that are, manifesting through them without error the cause in all things, and drawing out the soul's aspiration toward the divine; and what the air is in the sensible world, this in the world according to the understanding is courage, as a habit moving, and at once sustaining and effecting the innate life in spirit, and invigorating the soul's ever-moving about the divine; and what water is in the sensible world, this in the world of the understanding is temperance, being a habit productive of life-giving fruitfulness in spirit, and begetting the ever-welling yearning charm about the divine according to aspiration; and what earth is in the sensible world, this in the world of the understanding is justice, being a habit generative, according to form, of all the principles in the things that are, and apportioning to each, according to equality, the life-giving distribution in spirit, and the unchangeable establishment of its own base in the good, according to position.

⟦q19.11|1⟧ 96. ⟦q19.11|2⟧ Just as, when the flesh is in good condition and grows fat, the soul is tormented and darkened by the passions, as the habit of the virtues and the illumination of knowledge withdraw; so also, when the soul is guarded and made radiant by the divine beauty of the virtues and by the illumination of knowledge, *the outer man is corrupted*, [n: II Cor. iv, 16.] the flesh casting off its natural good condition through the sojourn of reason.

⟦q19.12|1⟧ 97. ⟦q19.12|2⟧ It was not possible otherwise for man, once he had come to be, to be shown son of God and God by the deification of grace, unless he were first born by choice by the Spirit, because of the self-moved and unmastered power naturally inhering in him. ⟦q19.12|2⟧ This deifying and divine and immaterial birth the first man abandoned, by preferring to the goods that are perceived by the mind and as yet unmanifest what is pleasant and manifest to sense; and he is condemned, fittingly, to have the coming-to-be from bodies, which is without choice and material and perishable.

⟦q19.13|1⟧ [1392] 98. ⟦q19.13|2⟧ Man is now moved either about irrational imaginations of passions, out of deceit, because of love of pleasure; or about the principles of the arts, out of distress, because of need; or about natural principles, out of the law of nature, because of learning: none of which drew man of necessity in the beginning, fittingly, since he had come to be above them all. ⟦q19.13|3⟧ For so it was fitting that he who was from the beginning should be: distracted in no way whatever by any of the things after him, or around him, or alongside him, and in need, for his perfection, of one thing alone, the motion without relation toward the one above him, I mean God, with the whole power of love.

⟦q19.14|1⟧ 99. ⟦q19.14|2⟧ The first man had nothing set between God and himself as a screen to knowing, and hindering the self-chosen kindredness that was to come about through love according to the motion toward God. ⟦q19.14|3⟧ For, being passionless by grace, he did not admit the deceit of the imagination of passions through pleasure; and, being in need of nothing, he was free of the necessity of distress about the arts because of need; and, being wise, he stood above the contemplation about nature because of knowledge.

⟦q19.15|1⟧ 100. ⟦q19.15|2⟧ God, who with wisdom gave subsistence to all nature, and secretly set the knowledge of himself in each of the rational essences according to its power, has given to us men too, as a munificent Master, the longing and yearning for himself according to nature, having naturally interwoven with it the power of reason; whereby we might be able with ease to know the modes of the fulfilment of the longing, and not, slipping aside, to miss what we strive to attain. ⟦q19.15|3⟧ Moved, then, by this longing, we are led on to seek concerning the truth itself, and the wisdom and governance that appear in good order in all things, eager through these to attain that for the sake of which we received the longing.

⟦q19.15|4⟧ *The end of the divine chapters of Maximus.*
